prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a rare case in which a quantitative theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, 2011) was followed years later by an experimental discovery (Jarillo-Herrero's group, 2018) of correlated insulators and superconductivity, and the pairing maps cleanly onto three credited names. It created a tunable platform for strongly correlated electrons that is now reproduced worldwide and has spread to other moire systems. In my own area, the appeal is that a minimal effective model organises a large and complicated phenomenology, which is the kind of conceptual economy I value. It also has the broadest opening support of the shortlist (four top-three placements, the highest Borda total), so choosing it is not an artefact of my own ranking.
statement.case_against: The field is only about eight years old and the origin of the superconductivity and of many correlated states is unsettled, so the committee risks rewarding a platform before its central physical lesson is known. Experimental credit is also shared with Cao and collaborators, who are outside the three-name limit, and the experimental discovery is a group result with several equally essential contributors. If the committee values maturity above breadth, optical lattice clocks (B002) are the safer choice.

responses.point: Eriksson places twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing that theory plus experiment is the decisive pairing and that independent reproduction by many groups makes the core interpretation stable despite the early timing.
responses.response: I now agree on ranking, which moves me from my opening, where I put KPZ first. I accept that the flat-band and correlated-insulator phenomenology is robust and independently reproduced. I would qualify the claim that the interpretation is stable: the flat-band origin is settled, but the pairing mechanism is not, and the citation should be worded around the discovery and the platform, not around an explanation of superconductivity. I also note that truncating the experimental credit to Jarillo-Herrero alone is a real attribution cost that we should state openly.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first: a clean Katori-Ye two-person attribution, mature and reproduced by many national laboratories, timely after the 2005 and 2012 prizes in related metrology.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case and I take it seriously. It wins on attribution clarity and maturity, and I disagree with my own earlier tendency to discount it as incremental. My difference is about conceptual novelty: the magic-wavelength idea is a very good enabling technique, but I judge the scientific discovery content of twisted bilayer graphene to be larger, because it opened an entirely new regime of correlated matter. I would not oppose B002 if the committee weights maturity more heavily, and I list it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and highlights that it is two decades old, independently confirmed, and underlies superconducting quantum processors, while acknowledging that attribution is split between theory and experiment across five people.
responses.response: I accept the maturity and impact argument for circuit QED. My reservation is attribution: the 2004 proposal and the 2004 strong-coupling experiment have five obvious contributors, and the three-person limit forces an exclusion of Blais or Wallraff that is hard to defend. Also, the 2025 prize already recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, so I would want to understand how much novelty margin remains. This is why I do not rank it above the graphene work, though I do not consider it weak.

responses.point: Olsson ranks spherical-aberration correction first as a clear instrument invention with the decisive trio of Rose, Haider and Urban and very wide lasting use across physics and materials science.
responses.response: The engineering achievement and its attribution are strong, and I agree the recognition is mature. My concern is whether it is physics discovery or enabling technology in the sense of the statutes, and whether Krivanek and the STEM-side correctors can be fairly omitted. I think that gap is greater than for the lattice-clock or graphene cases, so I leave it outside my configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges a field of about eight years, with an unsettled superconducting mechanism, to be mature enough.
How to treat the experimental credit shared with Cao and others outside the three-name limit.

Whether KPZ (my opening first choice) can be strengthened by a clearer attribution of the exact solutions and the random-matrix link; as listed it has little support and I am not pressing it as the preferred configuration.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile; I have no documented collaboration with any of the credited candidates, though KPZ touches random-matrix and stochastic-growth topics adjacent to my own research.
